So Jayon is working on a UGC-style product showcase video where he's already filmed himself in a top-down shot holding a Happy Day mango drink and a paper towel roll. He wants to swap out the background with a loft/studio space and replace the mango drink with a different product, though the request cuts off before specifying what that replacement is.

The real challenge here is that he's asking Seedance to handle multiple simultaneous swaps—background, product one, and product two—all from a single reference video. That's pushing against the principle of making one change per pass, which he's established in his own workflow. Using Seedance 2.0's reference video mode would inherit the actions and sound from his original footage, but I need to think through whether the model can realistically handle this many transformations at once without losing coherence.

The honest assessment is that this probably shouldn't be attempted as a single Seedance pass. Background replacement is fundamentally a compositing and rotoscoping problem—masking work or video-to-video restyle would be more appropriate. Product swaps are even trickier in video because the objects need to track with hand movement, match the lighting environment, and occlude correctly behind fingers. These are object replacement tasks that are genuinely difficult to execute cleanly in a generative model.

If I'm going to suggest using Seedance's reference system, I'd provide the original video as the performance driver, then reference images for the loft background and the two product swaps. But I'm doubtful this produces clean results in one pass. Given his own principle of "one change per pass," I should be honest about the limitations rather than hand him a prompt that won't work. The better strategy would be to separate these into distinct passes or reconsider the pipeline entirely—maybe starting with the first frame of the video and using image editing to establish the background and product swaps before generating from there.

Actually, that approach has a real problem: the products move throughout the video as he handles them, so a single edited first frame won't account for those position changes across the performance.

Looking at the timeline, the products appear at different moments—he starts without anything, then holds up the mango drink, then the paper towels. This means I need to handle multiple distinct segments, not just swap one frame and hope it carries through. The honest reality is that doing a full background replacement plus tracked product swaps across a moving performance with hand occlusion and proper lighting is pushing the limits of what Seedance can reliably do in one pass. Breaking this into segments or using a more targeted approach is probably the way forward.

The cleanest pipeline would be to split the video by beat—wherever a product appears or changes—then for each segment, create a locked first frame using an image editor where I swap both the background to the loft and the product in-hand to match what should be there. That gives Seedance a clear, correct anchor point. Then run each segment through Seedance with that edited frame plus the video reference, asking it to preserve his motion and performance while respecting the new background and product.

But actually, I'm second-guessing whether Seedance is even the right tool here. A talking head with background replacement is fundamentally a compositing problem—if he didn't shoot on green screen, I should handle the background removal and loft compositing in After Effects instead, which is cleaner and more precise than trying to get an AI video model to understand the composite intent.

The product swaps are what genuinely need AI. That said, he's explicitly asking to use Seedance as his reference, and I should respect his direction while being honest about the technical tradeoffs. Let me look at the actual stills and products he's provided to give him grounded advice rather than abstract recommendations.

Looking at the three reference images: the first shows him standing in his room with a kitchenette and colored door behind him, the second captures him holding up the mango juice carton at chest height, and the third shows him with a paper towel roll in his other hand. The products he wants to swap in are the Bio-Brühe jar, a new loft background, and the Bio Datteln pouch.

I'm realizing the core issue here: attempting three simultaneous swaps in a single Seedance pass from performance footage is risky and goes against his own principle of one change per pass. Plus, since the two products appear at different moments in the shot, this is really a multi-beat sequence rather than a single swap, which adds another layer of complexity.

Image-space editing with tools like Nano Banana Pro would give me much finer control for compositing than working in video-space, so I should lock down corrected frames first. For the background replacement on non-greenscreen footage, rotoscoping would keep him untouched, though I could also use Seedance with the loft as a reference if he wants to stay within his AI workflow.

The cleanest approach is to break this into frame-anchored segments in Premiere—splitting the reference video into distinct beats where I handle the intro separately, then tackle each product swap as its own focused moment rather than trying to cram everything into one pass.

For each beat's starting frame, I'd build a corrected composite in Nano Banana Pro using his three-reference workflow: the actual video frame for composition and identity, the loft image for background matching, and the new product image. The prompt would lock his pose and appearance while swapping the background to match the loft's high angle and lighting, plus replacing whatever product he's holding.

Then I'd feed each corrected frame as the first_frame anchor into Seedance along with the matching video segment, instructing it to follow his exact performance, motion, and audio while maintaining the new appearance I've established. After that, I'd reassemble everything and grade it.

The key insight is that Seedance can take both a first_frame and reference_video simultaneously—the first_frame locks the appearance while the reference_video drives all the motion and audio. That said, there's real risk that the product won't track perfectly with his hand movements across longer segments, and the background could drift or warp, especially if the camera is moving. I should note that shorter segments work better here—staying within that 3–10 second window he mentioned in his Kling notes, or Seedance's 4–15 second range—and flag that static, locked-off shots make background replacement much more stable than handheld footage.

For the background specifically, if his shot is static and high-angle, roto compositing the loft directly in After Effects or DaVinci would be cleaner and eliminate warping entirely—that's worth mentioning since he's already working in Premiere or Resolve anyway. Since the background should stay consistent across all the beats (same room), he'd use the same composited loft image for each one.

Before I hand you a prompt, one correction up front, because doing this the way it's described will fail: you're asking Seedance to invent three swaps at once (background + two products) from a moving performance video. That breaks your own one-change-per-pass rule, and worse — your two products appear at different moments, so this isn't one swap, it's a multi-beat shot. A single raw pass will warp the room and float the products in mismatched hand grips.

The principle that makes this work: lock every swap as a still image first, then let Seedance only carry motion. Image tools (Nano Banana Pro / gpt-image-2) are precise at compositing; video models are not. So you do the hard compositing where you're strong, and Seedance just propagates it across the clip.

Here's the pipeline:

Split the video by beat in Premiere — intro (no product), Beat 2 (mango carton up), Beat 3 (paper roll up). Keep each segment short, ideally under 8s.

Build a corrected first frame for each beat in Nano Banana Pro (your 3-ref workflow): Ref 1 = the actual video frame (identity/pose), Ref 2 = loft room (Image 5), Ref 3 = the new product. Directive prompt — replace background with the loft matched to the high top-down angle and lighting, replace the held product, and re-pose the gripping hand to naturally hold the new product's shape. This last part matters: the carton is tall, the Bio-Brühe jar is squat; the roll is fat, the dates pouch is flat. If you don't regenerate the grip, you get a jar sitting in a carton-shaped hand. One composite per beat, background stays the same loft across all of them.

Run each segment through Seedance with the corrected frame as first_frame and the video segment as reference_video. The first frame locks appearance; the video drives motion + timing.

Prompt template for the product beat (minimal, per your style):

@Video1 is the performance reference — match its motion, hand movement, and timing exactly. @Image1 is the exact first frame — start matching it perfectly and hold its background and product appearance for the entire clip.

Subject in the white quarter-zip raises the Bio-Brühe jar toward the high-angle camera, following the exact motion and timing of @Video1. Background stays the loft from @Image1, stable. Camera holds its high top-down angle.

Duration: [match segment] | Ratio: 16:9 | Resolution: 1080p | Audio: off

Swap the product line per beat. Note Audio: off —

On your audio: don't trust Seedance to reproduce your narration. Generate video only, keep your original recorded audio track, and relink it in Premiere. Because the prompt forces Seedance to preserve exact timing and motion, your real audio drops back in sync. That guarantees your voice is untouched — the most reliable "no problems" path.

One thing that changes the background step: is your camera locked off or moving? If it's static, skip generating the background entirely — roto yourself out in Resolve and composite the loft behind you. Rock-solid, zero warp, and your performance stays 100% real. The headline: there is no public Omni API yet

As of today (June 5, 2026), Gemini Omni Flash is real and launched, but it's a consumer/prosumer product, not an API. Omni Flash went live inside the Gemini app for U.S. subscribers across AI Plus, AI Pro, and AI Ultra tiers, and Google says it will roll out to developers via Vertex AI APIs "in the coming weeks." No public developer-facing model ID, no Gemini API or Vertex AI route, no pricing has been published in the official docs.

This matters directly to you because your access is API-only — you said you don't want the chat interface. Right now, the chat interface (Gemini app / Flow) is the only way to touch Omni. So the tool you're picturing — paste a prompt, choose resolution and duration, attach one reference video plus images — does not exist for Omni through any official Google API today.

A reality check on the "in the coming weeks" timeline: it's been said about multiple Google products. Gemini 3.5 Pro got a "June 2026" date and nothing else — no pricing, no API model ID, no specific release date beyond "June." Omni is in the same limbo. Plan around what exists, not the promise.

About those "Omni API" sites you'll find

If you search, you'll hit pages like EvoLink and WaveSpeed claiming a working Omni API with model IDs like gemini-omni-pro. Be careful — these are third-party aggregator/reseller routes, not Google. One of their own competitor analyses admits the truth: Google has officially introduced Gemini Omni, but there is no public Gemini API or Vertex AI model ID for Omni in the official developer docs — treat it as product momentum, not confirmed public API access. Another "API tutorial" site states outright that Gemini Omni has not been officially released, and their API code is based on Google's Vertex AI patterns and expected design — i.e., invented, not real. For a production short film, routing your footage and your face through an unofficial reseller is a data and reliability risk I'd avoid.

What Omni actually does (when it does land)

Worth knowing because it fits your exact use case well:

Reviewers call it "Nano Banana for video" — its strength is multi-turn iterative refinement, and it excels at remixing existing footage, restyling clips, extending segments, and reimagining scenes through natural language.

Google says Omni can keep the same characters, backgrounds, and movement consistent even after edits — which is the consistency problem that normally breaks video swaps.

It supports text, images, audio, and video clips as inputs, individually or combined — so you can provide a video clip alongside a text instruction and a reference image in the same prompt. That's precisely your background-plus-two-products scenario.

Two cautions for your specific shot:

The safety filter has heavy false positives on video input — clips that pass any reasonable general-audiences bar are getting blocked. A video of your own face could trip it.

Omni Flash is capped at 10-second clips, and every output carries a SynthID watermark and C2PA Content Credentials. Fine for a personal short, but know it's tagged as AI-generated.

What this means for your actual decision

The "one-go" dream — background swap plus both product swaps in a single Omni pass — isn't available to you via API right now. Two real paths:

If you want to try Omni now: the only door is the Gemini app / Flow chat interface, 10-second cap, on a paid AI tier. Conversational editing means you'd do it in turns anyway ("change the background to this room," then "replace the carton with this jar"), so it's iterative, not truly one-shot. That contradicts your API-only and one-go requirements, but it's the only way to touch the actual model today.

If you want to stay API-only: Omni is off the table until the Vertex route ships. The strongest API-documented path for reference-heavy work remains Seedance 2.0 — it has official ByteDance model materials, a published model card, and documented routes for text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video — which is exactly the layered pipeline I gave you last message. Google's own documented video API today is Veo 3.1, not Omni.

My recommendation: keep building on the locked-frame-plus-Seedance approach for this film, and set a reminder to re-check the Vertex AI docs in 2–3 weeks. The moment Google publishes a real model ID and pricing, Omni becomes a genuine one-pass option for the background + product swaps — and I can write you the proper API prompt structure then, once we know the actual input schema instead of guessing at it.

Want me to set up your current Seedance pipeline so it's structured to swap over to Omni cleanly when the API lands?

Good. Here's how the job actually maps onto Omni — and the order matters, because Omni's whole personality is conversational, turn-by-turn editing, not one giant prompt. You feed your real video as the base and then issue edits as a conversation, with the model holding everything else stable between turns. That's the "Nano Banana for video" part: each turn changes one thing and preserves the rest.

So your three swaps become three edit turns on top of your real footage:

Turn 0 — load the base. Upload your actual narrated video as the source clip. This is the anchor for motion, hand movement, your face, and audio. Don't describe the scene from scratch — Omni reads it.

Turn 1 — background.

Replace the room behind the person with this loft interior. Match the high top-down camera angle and the lighting on the subject. Keep the person, their motion, and the held objects exactly as they are.

Attach the loft room (Image 5) as a reference image. You confirm the result looks right before moving on — that's the point of the conversational model, you're not gambling on one pass.

Turn 2 — first product.

In the section where the person holds up the carton, replace the carton with this jar. Match how the hand grips it and keep the timing the same.

Attach the Bio-Brühe jar. Because Omni reasons about the scene, it should re-fit the grip to the jar's shape rather than floating it — the thing that breaks raw video swaps.

Turn 3 — second product.

In the section where the person holds the paper roll, replace it with this pouch. Keep the hand motion and timing.

Attach the Bio Dates pouch.

That's the realistic execution. A few hard constraints to design around:

The 10-second cap on Omni Flash is the real limiter. If your narrated take runs longer — and a two-product demo usually does — you can't do it in one clip. You'd split your video into sub-10s segments in Premiere, run each through Omni, then reassemble. Which, notice, is the same beat-splitting logic I gave you for Seedance. The pipeline doesn't actually change; only the engine does.

Your face on video input may trip the safety filter — that's the live false-positive problem right now. If a segment gets blocked, that's why, and there's no clean workaround except retrying or trimming.

Audio: Omni can preserve source audio, but for a narrated piece I'd still relink your original recorded track in Premiere rather than trust the model to keep your voice pristine. Same insurance as before.

And the unavoidable one: all of this is through the Gemini app / Flow chat interface today, not your API. There's no version of this that's API-only right now.
